newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels advance as army collapses in east.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels advance as army collapses in east.

text.p: Zairean rebels advanced on key government-controlled towns, following the trail of looting left by the government's ill-disciplined soldiers as they flee.

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), who control much of eastern Zaire, were by late Thursday advancing north and west towards the towns of Watsa and Isiro and the northeastern regional capital of Kisangani, Zaire's fourth largest city.
Worried authorities in the Zairean capital Kinshasa said demoralised soldiers were helping the cause of the rebels, backed by Rwanda, by alienating the local population.

Given the utter failure of the army in the war that began in October, some government officials privately see negotiations with guerrillas led by veteran opposition figure Laurent Kabila as the Zaire government's only way out.

"It is the same now as it was in Goma and Bukavu more than a month ago," a senior government official said. "The rebels announce they are coming days in advance. The soldiers loot the town and disappear, hardly putting up resistance."
The rebel advance now is targeting major Zairean towns in the east, such as Kisangani. Rebels claim to have taken the strategic mineral town of Kindu.
The chief editor of the local Catholic church radio station in Kisangani told Reuters there was no sign of rebels within 50 km (35 miles), but the army itself was the problem.
Deserting soldiers have been arriving in Kisangani in stolen aid vehicles. There are constant reports of rape and looting by the soldiers in the town and on roads from the eastern front.
Aid workers who left the city earlier this week said the army was spending more energy trying to disarm deserters who no longer obey any authority than on preparing for a rebel attack.
Analysts said the rebel advance had also been helped by Uganda's occupation of the Zairean border town of Kasindi in a campaign against alleged Ugandan rebels operating out of Zaire.
Ugandan troops were interviewed in Kasindi despite the assertion by Ugandan military spokesmen that troops only briefly pushed three km (two miles) into Zaire last week.

The Zairean rebels say their goal is to overthrow Zaire's ailing strongman Mobutu Sese Seko. Mobutu, absent from Zaire throughout the crisis, is currently recuperating from cancer treatment at his villa on the French Riviera.
The United States said on Wednesday it had warned the rebels not to set up a separate state in eastern Zaire and had urged Kabila to end alleged abuses by his troops of Rwandan refugees in Zaire.

"The United States is deeply concerned about the allegations of political murders and human rights abuses in eastern Zaire by elements of the rebel alliance," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.
"The United States will not support in any way, shape, or form any effort by the rebel alliance to try to create any kind of artificial state in eastern Zaire," he said.

The rebels have blocked deployment through their territory of a multinational force to help Rwandan refugees and Zaireans uprooted by the fighting since October, arguing that its real aim is to restore Mobutu's grip on power.

In Ottawa, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said the international coalition trying to deliver aid to eastern Zaire probably would not have to make food airdrops or intervene militarily in any major way.
